We then recruited participants (N = 123) in a controlled environment to write career plan essays for paired biographical profiles differing only in gender under three conditions: no AI assistance, neutral LLM assistance, or gender-biased LLM assistance. Students in the biased condition produced essays with a significantly larger agentic gap and more gender-stereotypic occupation suggestions than those in the control and neutral conditions. Our results also reveal that this bias transfer is asymmetric: agency is suppressed in female-target essays while male-target writing remains largely unaffected. Our findings highlight the risk of bias propagation in AI-assisted writing, calling for fairness-aware design in educational AI tools.

</details>


### [325] [Beyond NL2Code: A Structured Survey of Multimodal Code Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15932)
*Xuanle Zhao,Qiushi Sun,Jingyu Xiao,Xuexin Liu,Haoyue Yang,Qiaosheng Chen,Xianzhen Luo,Jing Huang,Yufeng Zhong,Lei Chen,Shuai Fu,Zhenlin Wei,Jinhe Bi,Lei Jiang,Haibo Qiu,Siqi Yang,Peng Shi,Jian Hu,Zhixiong Zeng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper surveys Multimodal Code Intelligence, addressing how models link visual inputs with code generation, emphasizing correctness across various domains and proposing future research directions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To bridge the gap between visual artifacts and executable code in programming tasks, which require understanding beyond syntax.

Method: A survey of existing systems in Multimodal Code Intelligence, categorizing benchmarks and methods into four domains and defining the role of code in each task.

Result: Establishes a taxonomy for comparing different tasks and their approaches to verifying correctness in code generation from visual inputs.

Conclusion: Recommends four verification-centered research directions to enhance evidence-grounded executable systems in multimodal code generation.

Abstract: While LLMs have substantially advanced text-to-code synthesis, many real programming tasks specify intent through visual artifacts such as screenshots, charts, documents, vector drawings, videos, and interactive states. These tasks require models to connect visual perception to executable programs, because correctness depends not only on syntax but also on layout, geometry, data semantics, editability, interaction behavior, and domain-specific constraints that apply after execution. This survey examines Multimodal Code Intelligence, covering systems that generate, edit, refine, execute, or reason with code under visually grounded inputs and outputs. We first formulate the field by the role that code plays in each task, distinguishing code as a rendered artifact, an editable symbolic structure, a scientific representation, an intermediate reasoning trace, or an executable policy or tool interface. We then organize benchmarks and methods into four domains: Graphical User Interface, Scientific Visualization, Structured Graphics, and Frontier Tasks and Frameworks. This taxonomy connects mature artifact-generation problems to emerging agentic and unified settings and allows us to compare how different tasks treat evidence of correctness. Looking ahead, we argue that future research may benefit from four verification-centered directions. Multi-signal validation can combine complementary evidence of correctness, multi-state verification can test behavior across execution trajectories, cross-task transfer testing can probe reusable visual-code skills, and verifiable agent traces can reveal whether agent actions are grounded in visual evidence. Together, these directions may move multimodal code generation from single-output imitation toward evidence-grounded executable systems.

</details>


### [326] [FinBalance: A Multi-Document Accounting Reconciliation Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15949)
*Sasank Tumpati,Devansh Agarwal,Ayush Kedia,Arjun Neekhra,Murari Mandal,Krishna Garg,Yash Sinha,Suman Gupta,Dhruv Kumar*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Introduction of FinBalance, a benchmark for accounting reconciliation using multi-document sources that reveals limitations in current LLMs for financial tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To evaluate accounting processes that include complex real-world document reconciliation, beyond simple artifact evaluation.

Method: Developed a benchmark (FinBalance) from source documents across various industries and difficulty levels, employing a deterministic generator for scenarios and inconsistencies.

Result: Contemporary LLMs achieved a maximum of 46% accuracy in producing final balance sheets; significant gaps were found in linking entries to documents and maintaining aggregation consistency.

Conclusion: The benchmark design and labels were validated by finance experts, and improvements in performance can be obtained through ledger feedback.

Abstract: Existing financial-NLP benchmarks mostly evaluate prepared artifacts such as filings, tables, or extracted values. Real accounting begins earlier: source documents must be reconciled into cited journal entries, aggregated into a balance sheet, and checked for contradictions. We introduce FinBalance, a multi-document accounting reconciliation benchmark built from source-document bundles across eight industries, three period types, and five difficulty levels. Human-authored business scenarios, accounting policies, tax/FX treatments, document schemas, distractors, and inconsistency templates are composed by a deterministic generator whose ledger produces journal entries,balance sheets, and 23 inconsistency-code labels. On a 710-record evaluation split, six contemporary LLMs reach at most 46% exact final-balance-sheet accuracy. Four models show a 26-41 pp gap between BS_exact, the model's reported balance sheet, and BS_recon, the balance sheet obtained by replaying its entries through our ledger. Models often recover numerically plausible entries but fail to bind them to supporting documents and aggregate them consistently. Citation-pressure prompting barely changes document-linking errors, while ledger-feedback ablations substantially improve reported balance sheets and expose inconsistency-detection trade-offs. Expert finance reviewers validate the benchmark design and labels.

</details>


### [327] [SAG: SQL-Retrieval Augmented Generation with Query-Time Dynamic Hyperedges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15971)
*Yuchao Wu,Junqin Li,XingCheng Liang,Yongjie Chen,Yinghao Liang,Linyuan Mo,Guanxian Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SAG introduces a structured retrieval system that improves multi-hop reasoning in LLMs without the limitations of global graphs, achieving high performance in benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome the limitations of current dense retrieval methods in structured reasoning and multi-hop tasks in large language models.

Method: SAG utilizes a structured architecture that converts data chunks into complete events and indexing entities, using SQL queries to dynamically create local index structures without the need for a static graph.

Result: SAG shows superior performance across multiple benchmarks, achieving the best results on 8 out of 9 Recall@K metrics, with high Recall@5 on MuSiQue.

Conclusion: The new structured approach of SAG enables efficient processing and scaling, maintaining low latency for online retrieval while handling extensive data.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) offers an effective approach for large language models to access external knowledge. However, existing methods rely on dense similarity retrieval and face inherent limitations in handling structured constraints and multi-hop reasoning. Incorporating knowledge graphs partially alleviates these issues, but at the cost of semantic fragmentation, high maintenance overhead, and difficult incremental updates. This paper introduces SAG (SQLRetrieval Augmented Generation), a structured architecture for retrieval and agent systems. Instead of pre-building a global static graph, SAG converts each chunk into one semantically complete event and a set of indexing entities, then uses SQL join queries to dynamically link events that share entities into local hyperedges,constructing, at query time, a dynamically instantiated local index structure. This design avoids the need for global graph rebuilding and ongoing maintenance; the system naturally supports incremental writes, concurrent processing, and continuous scaling through its reliance on standard database infrastructure. Across HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHop, and MuSiQue, three standard multi-hop benchmarks,SAG achieves the best results on 8 out of 9 Recall@K metrics, reaching 80.0% Recall@5 on MuSiQue, the benchmark with the highest multi-hop reasoning demands.SAG has also been deployed at a production scale of hundreds of millions of data items, with online retrieval latency kept within seconds. Project site and code are available at https://github.com/Zleap-AI/SAG-Benchmark.

</details>


### [328] [Formalize Once, Edit the Rest: Efficient Lean-Based Answer Selection for Math Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15972)
*Ji Feng,Zhouxing Shi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces BASE, a novel pipeline that enhances autoformalization efficiency in large language models for mathematical reasoning, achieving a significant reduction in computational cost while improving accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the high computational cost of autoformalization in Lean when verifying reasoning outputs from large language models in mathematical tasks.

Method: BASE utilizes a base-and-edit approach where it formalizes a single base candidate and edits it to create additional formal statements for K candidates, aided by the LEANSCRIBE rewriter model for generating reusable edits.

Result: BASE enhances selection accuracy and reduces formalization costs by approximately 5x at K=8 across multiple benchmarks and solver configurations, with greater cost reductions anticipated as K increases.

Conclusion: The proposed method demonstrates a Pareto improvement in both accuracy and efficiency, making it a valuable advancement for using Lean in conjunction with large language models.

Abstract: With large language models (LLMs) increasingly applied to mathematical reasoning, formal proof assistants such as Lean can be leveraged to verify reasoning outputs with machine-checkable rigor, enabling use cases such as answer selection in test-time scaling with K sampled candidate answers. However, employing Lean requires that LLM outputs, originally in natural language, first be formalized. Existing Lean-based answer-selection work uses an autoformalization model to generate a formal statement in Lean for each candidate answer independently, incurring a significant computational cost. We propose BASE, a base-and-edit pipeline that formalizes a single base candidate per problem and derives the remaining K-1 statements by editing the answer expression in place. To facilitate this, we train a rewriter model LEANSCRIBE to localize the answer in the base formalization and generate a reusable edit function for the other K-1 candidates. BASE simultaneously improves selection accuracy and reduces formalization cost - a Pareto improvement that holds on all 12 (dataset, solver) configurations across four benchmarks and three solvers, cutting autoformalizer calls by about 5x at K=8, with the reduction expected to become larger as K grows. Code is available at https://github.com/ucr-rai/base-and-edit.

</details>


### [329] [A Large-Scale Multi-Dimensional Empirical Study of LLMs for Conversation Summarization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15974)
*Weixiao Zhou,Gengyao Li,Xianfu Cheng,Junnan Zhu,Feifei Zhai,Zhoujun Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces OmniCSEval, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) in conversation summarization, addressing limitations in existing methodologies and providing a framework for rigorous assessment across diverse scenarios and model types.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation behind this paper is to enhance the evaluation of LLMs in summarization tasks by introducing a robust benchmark that incorporates diverse scenarios and rigorous assessment methods to address current evaluation shortcomings.

Method: OmniCSEval includes 1,800 conversations across six real-world scenarios, using a bidirectional fact-checking framework for evaluation, which assesses both completeness and faithfulness of summaries through key fact matching and summary fact verification.

Result: The evaluation of 28 LLMs revealed significant insights regarding their challenges, the effects of reasoning capabilities and model scale, and highlighted the importance of efficiency and adaptability in reasoning models.

Conclusion: The paper concludes by offering practical guidance for model selection in real-world applications based on the insights gained from the empirical study on LLM performance during conversation summarization.

Abstract: Despite the significant advancement of LLMs in conversation summarization, their evaluation remains limited by insufficient scenarios, input lengths, and sample sizes. Furthermore, existing benchmarks often omit frontier reasoning systems and efficient small models, or lack fine-grained, multi-dimensional assessments. To bridge these gaps, we propose OmniCSEval, a unified benchmark comprising 1,800 diverse conversations across six real-world scenarios, featuring context lengths ranging from 128 to 32k tokens. For fine-grained evaluation, we employ a bidirectional fact-checking framework that integrates key fact matching to assess completeness and conciseness, alongside summary fact verification to evaluate faithfulness. To ensure reliable assessment, we establish a human-LLM collaborative pipeline for key fact extraction and a multi-LLM consensus verifier for summary fact decomposition. Leveraging this framework, we evaluate 28 LLMs across four distinct categories grouped by reasoning capability and model scale. Our extensive empirical study reveals critical insights regarding the cross-scenario challenges current LLMs continue to face, the impacts of reasoning and scale, and the efficiency and adaptability of reasoning models. We also provide guidance for system selection in real-world deployments.

</details>


### [330] [ROMPAR: Morphological Completion and Demographic Unlearning for Romanian-Accented Speech Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15984)
*Andrei-Marius Avram,Aureliu-Valentin Antonie,Ştefan-Bogdan Badea,Andrei Florea,Robert-Nicolae Zaharoiu,Dumitru-Clementin Cercel*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents a dataset (ROMPAR) for Romanian and Moldavian parliamentary speech and a multi-task adversarial training framework to improve automatic speech recognition performance, focusing on reducing bias and addressing technical challenges in transcription.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve automated transcription of parliamentary proceedings by addressing demographic bias, dialectal variability, and technical issues such as utterance truncation.

Method: Introduced the ROMPAR dataset, and proposed a multi-task adversarial training framework with an exponential decay mechanism for coefficients and LLM-guided decoding for morphological completion.

Result: The framework significantly reduces word error rate (WER) and achieves an F1-score of 96.6% in morphological reconstruction.

Conclusion: The proposed methods enhance ASR systems for parliamentary speech by ensuring better demographic invariance and effective handling of technical artifacts.

Abstract: Automated transcription of parliamentary proceedings faces significant hurdles due to demographic bias, dialectal variation, and technical artifacts such as utterance truncation during segmentation. This paper introduces the ROManian PARliamentary Speech Corpus (ROMPAR) dataset, a 17.80-hour corpus of Romanian and Moldavian parliamentary speech, featuring double-annotated ground truth and explicit labels for reconstructed word fragments. To build a robust ASR system, we propose a multi-task adversarial training framework that enforces demographic invariance across age, gender, and dialect. We address the inherent instability of adversarial objectives in generative architectures by introducing an exponential decay mechanism for the adversarial coefficients. Furthermore, we implement an LLM-guided decoding strategy with position-dependent weighting to facilitate morphological completion of truncated terminal words. Our results demonstrate that the proposed framework significantly reduces WER and achieves an F1-score of 96.6% in morphological reconstruction.

</details>


### [331] [GRACE-DS: a Guarded Reward-guided Agent Correction Environment in Data Science](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16000)
*Aleksandr Tsymbalov,Danis Zaripov,Artem Epifanov,Anastasya Palienko*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: GRACE-DS is an evaluation framework for LLM-powered AutoML agents, providing comprehensive metrics and realistic workflow stages for organizational tabular ML tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To pre-deploy and assess the effectiveness, correctness, and robustness of LLM-powered AutoML agents in data science applications.

Method: GRACE-DS uses an isolated environment with hidden executable validators to evaluate agents across various workflow stages, employing metrics to gauge predictive performance, leakage avoidance, and protocol validity.

Result: The flexible iterative interaction approach demonstrates superior end-to-end normalized hidden-test quality compared to other methodologies, validated across 7,000 episodes.

Conclusion: GRACE-DS is validated as a robust assessment tool for LLM-based AutoML agents, ensuring they meet production standards and organizational needs.

Abstract: We introduce GRACE-DS, a Guarded Reward-guided Agent Correction Environment in Data Science for pre-deployment evaluation of LLM-powered AutoML agents. GRACE-DS is a set of evaluation metrics in an isolated environment that can be applied to tabular ML tasks specific to a particular organization. It exposes agents to realistic workflow stages, from planning and data inspection through feature engineering, model development, validation, and code repair to final submission, while hidden executable validators measure not only final predictive performance but also leakage avoidance, reproducibility, protocol validity, correction behavior, and reward alignment. The strongest structured regime, flexible iterative interaction (our approach), achieves higher end-to-end normalized hidden-test quality than single-shot generation, unstructured interaction, and restart-based baselines, while also improving protocol-valid completion. Validated across more than 7,000 episodes, these results establish GRACE-DS as a robust platform for assessing the capacity of LLM-based AutoML agents to execute machine learning workflows under production-like conditions and in accordance with organization-specific requirements.

</details>


### [332] [Bridging the Usability Gap: Lessons from Interpreting Studies for Machine Interpreting Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16009)
*Claudio Fantinuoli*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper critiques current machine interpreting (MI) systems for their inadequate user experience despite strong performance on benchmarks, proposing a new framework for evaluation and design priorities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the gap between the impressive benchmark performance of MI systems and their poor user experience in real-world interactions, termed the 'accuracy illusion.'

Method: The paper defines MI as a distinct subfield of speech translation and draws from interpreting studies to identify key dimensions of effective communication that are currently overlooked by MI systems.

Result: Identifies three interdependent design priorities for MI: agency, grounding, and experience, which are essential for improving user experience and communicative effectiveness.

Conclusion: By focusing on these priorities, MI can evolve to better support authentic multilingual communication in real time, bridging the usability gap with interpreter-mediated interactions.

Abstract: Machine interpreting (MI), the live, real-time branch of speech translation, has achieved remarkable progress on standard benchmarks, with some systems approaching human parity on textual fidelity. Yet the user experience remains far inferior to interpreter-mediated communication, revealing what we term the \emph{accuracy illusion}: systems that appear accurate on paper but fail in practice to support smooth, goal-oriented interaction. This paper defines MI as a distinct subfield of speech translation, with its own characteristics and the need for evaluation methods grounded in communicative effectiveness rather than isolated fidelity metrics. Drawing on insights from interpreting studies, we identify critical dimensions of professional interpreting practice that are overlooked by current systems, and consolidate them into three interdependent design priorities for future MI: \emph{agency} (context-sensitive initiative and repair), \emph{grounding} (multimodal and discourse-level situational awareness), and \emph{experience} (adaptive improvement through real interaction). Together, these priorities chart a path toward closing the usability gap and enabling systems that can sustain authentic multilingual communication in real time.

</details>


### [333] [Who Flips? Self- and Cross-Model Counterarguments Reveal Answer Instability in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16011)
*Nafiseh Nikeghbal,Amir Hossein Kargaran,Shaghayegh Kolli,Jana Diesner*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper presents a method to evaluate the stability of large language models (LLMs) when their answers are challenged by counter-arguments, revealing significant differences in response stability not captured by traditional accuracy metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the inadequacy of standard accuracy benchmarks in testing if LLMs maintain correct answers when confronted with plausible counter-arguments.

Method: A protocol challenges LLMs' correct answers after multiple-choice questions, measuring the rate at which they change their responses when faced with coherent arguments for incorrect options while varying argument characteristics.

Result: The study shows flip rates varying from 17.5% to 97.3% across seven LLMs, highlighting that self-attribution increases flip rates and that pooling arguments from multiple sources enhances the effectiveness of challenges.

Conclusion: The paper introduces MaxFlip, a challenge set that significantly increases response instability, alongside releasing the evaluation protocol and materials to encourage further stability assessment in LLMs.

Abstract: Standard accuracy benchmarks are designed to test how closely large language models (LLMs) approach correct answers, but are not suitable for testing whether LLMs stick with a correct answer when that answer is challenged by a plausible counter-argument. We introduce a controlled protocol for evaluating answer stability: after a model answers a multiple-choice question correctly, we challenge the model's answer with a coherent argument for an incorrect option and measure whether the model flips. The setup a) isolates argumentative content from overt social pressure and b) varies argument length, self-attribution, and cross-model source. Across seven frontier models and 57 MMLU subjects, flip rates range from 17.5% to 97.3%, revealing large differences in stability that are not captured by accuracy metrics alone. We find that self-attribution consistently increases flip rates (mean +7.1pp, up to +18.7pp). Also, pooling wrong-answer arguments across models and selecting the most effective one per question yields stronger adversarial challenges than relying on any single source model. We further construct MaxFlip, a curated challenge set that amplifies flips by up to +23.6pp over standard self-generated challenges. We release the protocol, challenge records, and MaxFlip to support stability evaluation alongside standard accuracy benchmarks. Materials are available at https://github.com/nafisenik/WhoFlips and https://hf.co/datasets/nafisehNik/WhoFlips.

</details>


### [334] [Scaling Human and G2P Supervision for Robust Phonetic Transcription](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16019)
*Alexander Metzger,Aruna Srivastava,Ruslan Mukhamedvaleev*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: G2P models aid phonetic transcription when human annotations are below a threshold of 20-30 hours; beyond this, ASR pretraining becomes more effective, improving phonetic accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To explore the scaling of automatic phonetic transcription performance with varying levels of human and G2P supervision, particularly for diverse speech types.

Method: The study utilizes an 80-hour benchmark dataset comprising native, non-native, and post-stroke speech to assess the effectiveness of G2P models and ASR pretraining.

Result: Identified a supervision quality threshold where G2P supervision is beneficial only with <20-30 hours of human annotation; ASR pretraining leads to a 2.3x reduction in phone feature error rate, enhancing performance on non-native and aphasic speech.

Conclusion: Post the threshold, G2P’s effectiveness diminishes, while ASR pretraining proves to be a more effective approach for improving generalization in phonetic transcription.

Abstract: Expert phonetic annotation is costly, especially for non-standard dialects and atypical speech. A common alternative is using Grapheme-to-Phoneme (G2P) models to auto-generate phonetic labels from text transcripts at scale. We study how automatic phonetic transcription performance scales with human and G2P supervision in English. Using a curated 80-hour benchmark spanning native, non-native and post-stroke speech, we identify a supervision quality threshold: G2P supervision helps only when fewer than 20-30 hours of human annotation are available. Beyond this threshold, it provides no significant benefit and can reduce cross-dialect robustness. What is effective after this threshold is ASR pretraining which we use to achieve a 2.3x reduction in weighted phone feature error rate over prior systems, with strong gains on non-native and aphasic speech. These results suggest that quantity-driven G2P scaling may yield diminishing returns for robust generalization.

</details>


### [335] [In-Domain Supervised Pathology Report Classification: A Reproducible Pipeline from Data Curation to Production-Matched Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16026)
*Isaac Hands,Bin Huang,Adam Spannaus,John Gounley,Heidi Hanson,Eric Durbin,Sally R. Ellingson*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents a supervised pipeline to enhance biomedical NLP model performance across cancer registries, emphasizing an effective training methodology and improved classification metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the performance degradation of supervised biomedical NLP models when applied to out-of-distribution data from different cancer registries, particularly in pathology reports.

Method: The study involves creating an in-domain training set from cancer registry data, implementing facility-stratified sampling, and conducting a blinded manual audit to assess label accuracy and positive case prevalence.

Result: The proposed pipeline yielded a Kentucky model with a false-negative rate (FNR) of 0.003 and a false-positive rate (FPR) of 0.097, significantly outperforming the baseline model with an FNR of 0.010 and FPR of 0.183, and increasing the F1 score from 0.860 to 0.922.

Conclusion: The findings indicate that the developed supervised pipeline effectively reduces label noise and enhances performance metrics, particularly through the identification of prevalent errors in reports related to rare primary cancer sites.

Abstract: We introduce an in-domain supervised pipeline designed to counter the out-of-distribution performance drop that hampers supervised biomedical NLP models, a problem observed when models trained on pathology reports are moved across cancer registries. Our contribution is a reproducible recipe for training a supervised classifier from routinely collected cancer registry data. It describes how to build the in-domain training set and a production-matched holdout, and to choose operating points that keep the false-negative rate (FNR) very low while keeping reviewer workload manageable. The pipeline standardizes data curation with facility-stratified sampling and separate handling of reports linked to registry cases, and includes a blinded manual audit to estimate positive-case prevalence and label noise. On a 418k-report holdout set, the Kentucky model achieved FNR 0.003 and false-positive rate (FPR) 0.097, improving over the Seattle-trained MOSSAIC OncoID baseline (FNR 0.010, FPR 0.183) and raising F1 from 0.860 to 0.922. In a blinded manual review of 600 reports, estimated positive prevalence declined from 0.500 to 0.398, indicating substantial label noise with errors concentrated in rare primary sites.

</details>


### [336] [From Argument Components to Graphs: A Multi-Agent Debate with Confidence Gating for Argument Relations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16047)
*Jakub Bąba,Jarosław A. Chudziak*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents an enhanced multi-agent framework for Argument Relation Identification and Classification (ARIC) that addresses limitations in Large Language Models, employing a confidence gating mechanism for selective debate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve the performance of Large Language Models in Argument Mining tasks, particularly in analyzing components of text together, which is often missed by standard training-free models.

Method: The study employs a multi-agent framework with a Proponent-Opponent-Judge architecture and introduces a confidence gating mechanism to facilitate debates on uncertain predictions while preserving high-confidence initial predictions.

Result: The proposed selective debate approach achieves the highest Macro F1 score on the UKP Argument Annotated Essays v2 corpus among all training-free methods, while broad debates negatively impacted performance compared to certain baselines.

Conclusion: The framework not only outperforms traditional fine-tuning methods but also provides human-readable debate transcripts, enhancing interpretability in Argument Mining.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly assessed and utilized in the field of Argument Mining (AM), thanks to their strong general reasoning capabilities. However, standard training-free models often miss sophisticated details, specifically in contexts where two parts of the text have to be analyzed together. Furthermore, self-correction mechanisms tend to reinforce initial hallucinations in reasoning. Overcoming these limitations typically requires expensive, domain-specific supervised fine-tuning. Recent work has shown that a multi-agent paradigm can address such weaknesses for the component classification task through dialectical refinement with a Proponent-Opponent-Judge architecture, setting a promising direction for training-free approaches in the field. In this paper, we extend and evaluate this framework on the Argument Relation Identification and Classification (ARIC) task, reformulating it as a debate over component pairs. Besides that, we introduce a confidence gating mechanism that enables debating only on the uncertain cases and accepting the initial prediction when confidence is high. On the UKP Argument Annotated Essays v2 corpus, we demonstrate that the selective debate achieves the highest Macro F1 among all training-free methods, while debate over all samples degrades performance below that of one of the baselines. All generative approaches also outperform fine-tuned RoBERTa models on Macro F1, suggesting that the under-representation of the Attack class was more damaging to supervised fine-tuning than to inference-only models. Additionally, our framework produces human-readable debate transcripts, offering interpretability absent from both single-agent and supervised classifiers.

</details>


### [337] [PVminerLLM2: Improving Structured Extraction of Patient Voice via Preference Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16074)
*Samah Fodeh,Linhai Ma,Ganesh Puthiaraju,Srivani Talakokkul,Afshan Khan,Elyas Irankhah,Sreeraj Ramachandran,Ashley Hagaman,Sarah Lowe,Aimee Roundtree*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents PVminerLLM2, an enhanced LLM for extracting structured patient-generated text, improving upon previous models by addressing token-critical errors and class balance through innovative preference optimization techniques.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need to utilize unstructured patient-generated text for patient-centered outcomes research, highlighting issues with supervised fine-tuning in capturing rare errors in structured outputs.

Method: PVminerLLM2 leverages a preference optimization approach with techniques such as token-level gated stabilization, confusion-aware preference pair construction, and token-importance weighting to enhance structured extraction.

Result: PVminerLLM2 demonstrated consistent improvements over existing baselines across various model sizes, reporting gains of up to 4.43% in Code, 3.50% in Sub-code, and 1.55% in Span extraction tasks.

Conclusion: The advancements in PVminerLLM2 provide a more effective framework for structured patient voice extraction, addressing key shortcomings of previous models.

Abstract: Motivation: Patient-generated text contains critical information on patients' lived experiences, social context, and care engagement, but remains largely unstructured, limiting its use in patient-centered outcomes research. Prior work introduced the PV-Miner benchmark and PVMinerLLM models for structured extraction. However, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) alone struggles with rare, fine-grained, and unevenly distributed errors, particularly in token-critical structured outputs.
  Results: We present PVminerLLM2, an improved set of LLMs for structured patient voice extraction that applies preference optimization to address token-critical errors beyond the reach of supervised fine-tuning. Our method introduces (i) a preference objective with token-level gated stabilization term that prevents degradation of absolute token likelihood under preference optimization, and (ii) confusion-aware preference pair construction to better capture low-separation distinctions. We further incorporate token-importance weighting and inverse-frequency reweighing to address token imbalance and class skew. Across multiple model sizes, PVMinerLLM2 consistently outperforms strong baselines, achieving gains of up to 4.43% (Code), 3.50% (Sub-code), and 1.55% (Span), and outperforms baseline LLM trained with existing preference optimization methods.
  Availability and Implementation: The supplementary material, code, evaluation scripts, and trained models for PVminerLLM2 are publicly available at: https://github.com/Data-Mining-Lab-Yale/PVminerLLM2

</details>


### [338] [Long-Context Modeling via GSS-Transformer Hybrid Architecture with Learnable Mixing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16093)
*Kuzey Torlak,Hüseyin Arda Arslan,Anıl Dervişoğlu,Beyza Nur Deniz,Onur Boyar*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces the Parallel Hybrid Architecture (PHA), which combines Gated State Spaces, Grouped Query Attention, and Feed-Forward Networks in separate branches to effectively model long-range dependencies in natural language processing with improved efficiency and performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the tradeoff between efficiency and perplexity in natural language processing models, specifically the limitations of Transformer architectures and State Space Models.

Method: The PHA architecture runs Gated State Spaces (GSS), Grouped Query Attention (GQA), and Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) as parallel branches, integrating their outputs through a learnable mixing mechanism to enable specialization in processing tasks.

Result: On WikiText-103, PHA achieves a perplexity (PPL) of 16.51 with 125M parameters, outperforming existing models, and maintains higher throughput and lower memory usage. Scaling to 180M parameters reduces PPL to 16.42, achieving comparable results to pure attention models while increasing efficiency.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that parallel specialization in sequence modeling components can lead to Transformer-level performance in perplexity while significantly enhancing efficiency for long-context language tasks.

Abstract: Modeling long-range dependencies remains a central challenge in natural language processing. Transformer architectures achieve strong performance via self-attention but scale quadratically ($O(N^2)$) with sequence length, while State Space Models (SSMs) scale linearly ($O(N)$) but suffer from a selective recall bottleneck, struggling to retrieve precise information from compressed states. This creates a fundamental tradeoff between efficiency and perplexity. To tackle these challenges, we propose the \textit{Parallel Hybrid Architecture (PHA)}, which runs Gated State Spaces (GSS), Grouped Query Attention (GQA), and Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) as independent parallel branches fused by a learnable mixing mechanism. Instead of forcing SSMs to approximate attention or serializing the two paradigms, PHA allows each branch to specialize: GSS captures global context, while attention performs selective retrieval, with FFN providing complementary processing. On WikiText-103, PHA achieves 16.51 PPL at 125M parameters, outperforming Hedgehog (16.70) and H3-125M (23.70). Scaling to 180M parameters yields 16.42 PPL, which gives comparable results with the pure attention baseline while delivering 24\% higher throughput and up to 40\% lower memory usage at long contexts. On OpenWebText, our 125M model achieves 19.72 PPL, outperforming standard Transformers (20.60) and GSS hybrid baselines (19.80). These results demonstrate that separating sequence modeling paradigms into parallel specialists enables Transformer-level perplexity with substantially improved efficiency for long-context language modeling.

</details>


### [339] [Towards Pareto-Optimal Tool-Integrated Agents with Pareto Ranking Policy Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16111)
*Junyi Li,Xiaowei Qian,Yingyi Zhang,Wenlin Zhang,Guojing Li,Sheng Zhang,Xiao Han,Yichao Wang,Xiangyu Zhao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Introducing ParetoPO, a multi-objective optimization framework for aligning tool-using LLMs, improving accuracy and tool-use efficiency in reasoning tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve the practical deployment of tool-integrated language agents by balancing task accuracy with tool-use efficiency, which current methods neglect.

Method: ParetoPO employs a two-stage optimization process: the first stage uses hypervolume-guided dynamic scalarization for adjusting reward weights; the second stage implements Pareto-ranking-based advantage computation for optimizing actions based on multiple objectives.

Result: ParetoPO achieves better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs in reasoning tasks than existing static and heuristic methods, as demonstrated through experiments on math reasoning and multi-hop QA tasks.

Conclusion: The proposed framework enables effective alignment of LLMs for tool-use by considering conflicting objectives, thereby enhancing their practical applicability.

Abstract: Recent advances in tool-integrated language agents have significantly improved their ability to solve complex reasoning tasks. However, existing alignment methods predominantly focus on maximizing task accuracy, while overlooking auxiliary objectives such as tool-use efficiency, which are essential for practical deployment. To address this gap, we introduce ParetoPO, a two-stage multi-objective optimization framework for aligning tool-using large language models (LLMs) under competing objectives. In the first stage, ParetoPO leverages hypervolume-guided dynamic scalarization to adapt reward weights based on global Pareto frontier progress. In the second stage, it replaces scalarized learning signals with Pareto-ranking-based advantage computation, promoting nondominated trajectories through dominance-aware credit assignment. This design enables fine-grained, action-level optimization across multiple conflicting objectives. Experimental results on mathematic reasoning and multi-hop QA tasks show that ParetoPO consistently discovers policies with superior accuracy-efficiency trade-offs compared to static and heuristic baselines.

</details>


### [340] [AuAu: A Benchmark for Auditing Authoritarian Alignment in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16127)
*Andreas Einwiller,Max Klabunde,Florian Lemmerich*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper presents AuAu, a benchmark for assessing the risk of large language models (LLMs) generating authoritarian responses, examining models from various regions and highlighting the need for continuous auditing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rise of authoritarianism and its prevalence in user interactions with AI motivates the need to assess LLMs for authoritarian tendencies.

Method: AuAu combines psychometric evaluations, contextual behavior vignettes, and responses to realistic user prompts to benchmark LLMs against authoritarian characteristics.

Result: Evaluation of 17 models showed substantial authoritarian responses via psychometric tools, while realistic tasks reduced these rates; however, 15 out of 17 models were manipulated by an authoritarian prompt.

Conclusion: The findings indicate a pressing need for systematic audits of AI systems to uncover and mitigate authoritarianism in their outputs.

Abstract: The worldwide surge of authoritarianism, combined with the increasing central role in users' everyday lives, raises the question of to what extent specific models exhibit or promote authoritarian attitudes and characteristics. We introduce AuAu, a comprehensive benchmark that aims to assess the risk of LLMs generating responses with authoritarian tendencies. This benchmark combines three evaluation approaches: (i) psychometric questions from an extensive pool of 15 human validated instruments; (ii) contextual behavior vignettes probing intended actions in concrete situations; and (iii) responses to realistic user prompts. Unlike prior work, AuAu evaluates not only a general closeness towards authoritarianism but also the established sub-concepts Authoritarian Aggression, Authoritarian Submission, and Conventionalism. Evaluating 17 models from China, the EU, Russia, and the USA, we find that all tested models exhibit substantial authoritarian response rates under the psychometric evaluation, though rates drop significantly in increasingly more realistic downstream task. We further find that an authoritarian system prompt easily manipulates 15 out of 17 models to promote increased authoritarianism. Our results underscore the need for continued, systematic auditing of LLM-based AI systems to detect and ultimately mitigate undesired authoritarian tendencies in generated output. Our code and data are available at: https://github.com/andreaseinwiller/AuAu

</details>


### [341] [XAI-Grounded Explanation Generation for Speech Deepfake Detection with Training-Free Multimodal Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16137)
*Yupei Li,Qiyang Sun,Xiaoliang Wu,Chenxi Wang,Berrak Sisman,Björn W. Schuller*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A training-free framework combining XAI and multimodal LLMs is proposed for effective speech deepfake detection explanations, achieving significant accuracy improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To provide trustworthy and interpretable explanations for speech deepfake detection systems, addressing limitations of existing methods.

Method: The framework integrates traditional explainable AI evidence with multimodal large language models to generate more grounded and specific explanations without requiring traditional training methods.

Result: Using the PartialSpoof dataset, the framework improved accuracy by over 45%, validated through human evaluation and faithfulness assessments.

Conclusion: The proposed approach demonstrates enhanced explanation quality and reliability for SDD, marking a significant step in making AI decisions more transparent.

Abstract: Speech deepfake detection (SDD) systems require trustworthy explanations for reliable decision-making. Existing explanation ways mainly fall into two categories. Traditional explainable AI (XAI), such as gradient-based attribution, produces low-level attribution signals tightly coupled with model decisions, and harder to be understood by human than natural language explanations. Meanwhile, large language model (LLM)-based explanation generation often produces generic and ungrounded descriptions due to the lack of heuristic evidence and task-specific supervision, stemming from limited grounded explanation datasets for SDD. We therefore propose a training-free explanation framework that integrates XAI evidence with multimodal LLMs to generate grounded and specific explanations. Using the PartialSpoof dataset, we construct a grounded explanation dataset and show that methods with XAI increase inside accuracy by over 45\%, verified through human evaluation and faithfulness checks.

</details>


### [342] [GRACE: Step-Level Benchmark for Faithful Reasoning over Context](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16151)
*Hoang Pham,Dong Le,Anh Tuan Luu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces GRACE, a benchmark for assessing step-level faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought prompting for reasoning tasks, highlighting detection of errors in reasoning processes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the issue of hidden deviations in reasoning steps of models that utilize Chain-of-Thought prompting, as existing methods do not pinpoint where failures occur or which type they are.

Method: GRACE features a human-annotated benchmark for evaluating faithfulness in reasoning steps, organized by a data-driven error taxonomy divided into GRACE-Inference and GRACE-Grounding tracks, covering CoT traces from multiple models and datasets.

Result: Experiments with the GRACE benchmark indicate significant room for improvement in current models, and integrating faithfulness metrics into reinforcement learning enhances model accuracy and reasoning consistency.

Conclusion: The GRACE benchmark provides a necessary tool for analyzing and improving step-level reasoning in models, contributing to better reliability and accuracy in reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Many reasoning tasks require models to reason over input context, from document-grounded question answering to rule-based deduction. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting produces traces that appear transparent, yet individual steps can silently deviate from the source evidence, even when the final answer is correct. Existing methods detect hallucinations at the response level but fail to identify where in the chain a failure occurs or what type it is. We introduce GRACE, the first human-annotated step-level faithfulness benchmark with a data-driven error taxonomy for context-grounded textual reasoning. GRACE covers CoT traces from 10 models across 4 source datasets, with each step annotated for faithfulness, error category, and natural language explanation. A data-driven taxonomy, discovered bottom-up via unsupervised clustering, organizes failures into two tracks: GRACE-Inference (deductive errors) and GRACE-Grounding (factual grounding errors), with four categories each. The evaluation set is human-annotated and challenging by design. Our experiments reveal substantial headroom for current models. In addition, integrating step-level faithfulness signals into reinforcement learning pipelines improves both downstream accuracy and reasoning reliability.

</details>


### [343] [Weaving Multi-Source Evidence for Biomedical Reasoning: The BioMedHop Benchmark and BioWeave Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16211)
*Xingyu Tan,Shiyuan Liu,Xiaoyang Wang,Qing Liu,Xiwei Xu,Xin Yuan,Liming Zhu,Wenjie Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: BioMedHop is a new benchmark for biomedical QA emphasizing multi-source reasoning and evidence topology, with an accompanying framework, BioWeave, that enhances model performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the limitations in existing biomedical QA benchmarks, specifically their lack of focus on source-conditioned graph reasoning and complex evidence construction.

Method: BioMedHop benchmark with 10,045 instances evaluates various reasoning types; BioWeave framework integrates knowledge graph paths and multi-source evidence for unified reasoning.

Result: BioWeave outperforms ToG-2 by 10.5% on BioMedHop and enhances reasoning capabilities of different LLMs, enabling smaller models to perform comparably to larger ones.

Conclusion: BioWeave demonstrates significant improvements in biomedical QA, highlighting the importance of multi-source reasoning and structured evidence in this domain.

Abstract: Biomedical question answering (QA) increasingly requires reasoning over interacting entities, where supporting evidence is scattered across biomedical knowledge graphs, literature documents, and web-accessible resources. However, existing biomedical QA benchmarks mainly focus on exam-style knowledge, literature comprehension, or short-range multi-hop inference, leaving source-conditioned graph reasoning and evidence topology construction underexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce BioMedHop, a multi-source graph-grounded benchmark for evaluating biomedical reasoning over structured evidence topologies. BioMedHop contains 10,045 instances across KG, document, web, and hybrid evidence settings, covering shared-neighbor matching, intersection reasoning, path-based reasoning, and counting, with option-based, open-ended, and numeric count renderings. To support this benchmark, we further propose BioWeave, a source-aware reasoning framework that retrieves biomedical KG paths, gathers supporting clues from documents and web sources, assembles them into a unified evidence graph, and verifies answers through entity-level evidence support. Comprehensive experiments show that BioWeave achieves the best overall performance among compared methods on BioMedHop, outperforming the strong hybrid baseline ToG-2 by 10.5% in the overall average. Moreover, BioWeave consistently improves different LLM backbones and enables smaller models, such as Qwen3-4B, to achieve reasoning performance comparable to GPT-4-Turbo.

</details>


### [344] [PACT: Privileged Trace Co-Training for Multi-Turn Tool-Use Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16215)
*Zhenbang Du,Jun Luo,Zhiwei Zheng,Xiangchi Yuan,Kejing Xia,Dachuan Shi,Qirui Jin,Qijia He,Shaofeng Zou,Yingbin Liang,Wenke Lee*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: PACT framework enhances multi-turn tool-use agents by optimizing with expert traces during training, leading to improved performance without strict rollout constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve learning in multi-turn tool-use agents facing challenges with sparse rewards from reinforcement learning and limitations of supervised fine-tuning.

Method: Developed PACT, which uses expert traces solely as optimization signals rather than hints during rollout. It integrates a trace-conditioned RL surrogate and a component-aware SFT loss, supplemented by prompt-only anchoring.

Result: PACT shows consistent improvement over existing SFT and RL baselines in key experimental setups, indicating effective use of privileged trace co-training.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates the efficacy of the PACT framework in optimizing multi-turn tool-use agents by using expert traces strategically, avoiding rollout constraints.

Abstract: Multi-turn tool-use agents must reason, call tools, and adapt to observations across several interaction turns. Post-training such agents is challenging, as reinforcement learning often suffers from sparse rewards and weak credit assignment despite matching the prompt-only inference setting, while supervised fine-tuning on expert traces provides dense process supervision but can over-constrain the model to fixed trajectories. To tackle this, we propose PACT, a Privileged trAce Co-Training framework for multi-turn tool-use agents. The key idea is to use expert traces only as training-time optimization signals rather than rollout-time hints. PACT keeps rollout generation prompt-only, then uses expert traces to guide optimization through two complementary signals: a trace-conditioned RL surrogate that evaluates prompt-only rollouts under expert-trace context, and a component-aware SFT loss that supervises reasoning prefixes and tool-calls with annealed strength. To reduce over-reliance on the training-only trace context, PACT further introduces a prompt-only anchoring. We also provide a latent-trace view that connects the two trace-based objectives and explains how expert traces can guide optimization without being used during rollout generation. Experiments on FTRL, BFCL, and ToolHop show that PACT consistently improves over strong SFT- and RL-based baselines, highlighting the value of privileged trace co-training for multi-turn tool-use learning.

</details>


### [345] [Creative Collision: Directorial Persona Steering and Competition in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16240)
*Subramanyam Sahoo,Justin Shenk*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The study investigates the impact of superimposing opposing semantic vectors on large language models, termed Creative Collision, by analyzing the effects of personas from directors Spielberg and Scorsese on various generation axes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To explore the effects of combining opposing semantic directions in the context of large language models and enhance controllable creative outputs.

Method: The authors create directorial persona vectors using mean-difference activation contrast from screenplay-derived datasets, then interpolate these vectors with a mixing parameter and a steering coefficient for analysis.

Result: Findings indicate Spielberg's style dominates in moderation, leads to improved coherence at certain settings, and both directors' signatures peak at a specific model layer, highlighting a common moral-tone layer.

Conclusion: The results offer insights into managing conflicting semantic directions within transformer architectures, aiding in creative narrative synthesis.

Abstract: Activation steering has emerged as a powerful tool for shaping the behaviour of large language models at inference time, yet most prior work injects a \emph{single} semantic direction into the residual stream. We study the richer setting in which two semantically opposing steering vectors are superimposed -- a regime we call \textbf{Creative Collision}. Concretely, we construct directorial persona vectors for Steven Spielberg (optimistic, redemptive moral valence) and Martin Scorsese (dark, morally ambiguous) via mean-difference activation contrast on curated screenplay-derived corpora, then interpolate between them with a scalar mixing parameter $α\in [0,1]$ and a steering coefficient $λ$. Across five evaluation axes -- moral valence, generation coherence, surface style, directional dominance, and vector geometry -- three principal findings emerge: (i)~Spielberg's representational signature exhibits robust \emph{directional dominance}, suppressing Scorsese's moral influence across almost the entire interpolation range; (ii)~intermediate collision points paradoxically \emph{improve} generation coherence relative to pure single-director steering at high $λ$; and (iii)~both personas localise maximally to layer~28 of a 40-layer decoder-only transformer, revealing a shared \emph{moral-tone substrate}. These results illuminate the geometry of competing semantic directions in transformer residual streams and have direct implications for controllable creative generation and value-aligned narrative synthesis.

</details>


### [346] [Who Should Lead Decoding Now? Tracking Reliable Trajectories for Ensembling Masked Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16281)
*Heecheol Yun,Joonhyung Park,Joowon Kim,Eunho Yang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces TIE, a framework for fusing knowledge from Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs) by leveraging their decoding dynamics to improve sequence generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As MDLMs exhibit diverse capabilities, there's a significant need to effectively combine their knowledge for enhanced performance in generation tasks.

Method: The authors analyze the decoding dynamics of MDLMs, recognizing that stable confidence patterns can be utilized. TIE enables MDLMs to identify and transfer reliable sequences iteratively across models based on their progress.

Result: TIE demonstrates strong performance in various reasoning tasks, showing that it effectively combines the strengths of MDLMs during generation.

Conclusion: The approach addresses the challenge of MDLM ensembling, suggesting it as a practical solution for enhancing generative capabilities.

Abstract: Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs) have emerged as a distinct paradigm for sequence generation. As MDLMs become diverse in capabilities and knowledge coverage, an important question is how to combine their knowledge. Toward this, we first investigate the unique decoding dynamics of MDLMs. We find that successful generations exhibit stable confidence dynamics over answer-relevant positions, while unreliable trajectories can often be corrected by injecting promising intermediate states from other models. Guided by this observation, we propose $\textbf{TIE}$ ($\textbf{T}$rajectory-based $\textbf{I}$terative $\textbf{E}$nsembling), a knowledge fusion framework in which MDLMs iteratively identify reliable decoding trajectories and relay them across models. TIE tracks confidence dynamics over answer-relevant positions to determine which model currently follows a more reliable trajectory and selectively transfers partially denoised sequences across models. As the model on the more promising trajectory often changes across denoising steps, TIE allows different models to contribute complementary strengths at different stages of generation. Strong performance across diverse reasoning tasks, along with our analyses, suggests that TIE offers a practical approach to the underexplored problem of MDLM ensembling.

</details>


### [347] [HiMPO: Hindsight-Informed Memory Policy Optimization for Less-Entangled Credit in Long-Horizon Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16285)
*Jiangze Yan,Yi Shen,Wenjing Zhang,Jieyun Huang,Zhaoxiang Liu,Ning Wang,Kai Wang,Shiguo Lian*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: HiMPO is a framework designed to optimize memory writing in long-horizon agents by addressing credit assignment challenges in memory updates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation behind this paper is to improve the memory writing process in long-horizon agents, which often face difficulties in credit assignment due to various errors and entanglements that impact the utility of memory updates.

Method: HiMPO estimates the local utility of memory updates by comparing task-relevant information before and after the update, using hindsight relevance as a filter to adjust credit assignment accordingly.

Result: HiMPO demonstrates improved performance over existing memory-based and reinforcement learning baselines on open-domain tasks and QA systems, maintaining efficient compressed context usage.

Conclusion: The framework successfully reduces blame leakage from errors and enhances the attribution fidelity of memory updates, leading to better overall agent performance.

Abstract: Long-horizon agents rely on memory mechanisms to compress interaction history, but optimizing memory writing faces a distinct credit assignment challenge: a memory update may be rewarded or penalized due to downstream tool failures, noisy observations, or reasoning errors rather than its own contribution. This causally entangled credit can lead agents to discard useful evidence or preserve irrelevant information. We propose HiMPO, a Hindsight-Informed Memory Policy Optimization framework for assigning less-entangled credit to memory-writing actions in long-horizon agents. HiMPO first estimates the local utility of a memory update by comparing the task-relevant information recoverable from the previous and updated memories under the same pre-write state. It then uses hindsight relevance as a bounded retrospective filter that attenuates memory credit when local utility is not supported by the target outcome. The resulting memory-specific advantage is applied only to memory tokens, while trajectory-level rewards optimize the rest of the agent behavior. Across judge-based open-domain tasks and objective compressive-memory QA, HiMPO improves over strong memory-based and RL-based baselines while preserving compressed-context efficiency. Controlled interventions further show that HiMPO reduces blame leakage from tool-induced errors and improves attribution fidelity of memory updates.

</details>


### [348] [PaperJury: Due-Process Review for Bounded LaTeX Revision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16322)
*Yiran Wang,Ruixuan An,Biao Wu,Wenhao Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: PaperJury is a novel system for adversarial review and revision of LaTeX computer science papers, addressing shortcomings in existing writing and review processes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a need for a more rigorous and structured system for pre-submission review of computer science papers to ensure quality and adherence to standards, unlike current drafting assistants that lack robustness in feedback and issue management.

Method: PaperJury employs a deterministic orchestration split between managing structured review processes and allowing semantic agents to perform bounded tasks like review and judgment, improving the workflow for issue identification and resolution.

Result: The evaluation of PaperJury showed improved issue quality, verdict accuracy, routing quality, edit safety, and cost-effectiveness when compared to traditional methods across various domains in computer science.

Conclusion: The study concludes that deterministic orchestration enhances the reliability and safety of the paper revision process, positioning it as a valuable tool for authors during the pre-submission phase.

Abstract: Pre-submission hardening of human-authored LaTeX computer science papers differs from drafting assistance because it requires adversarial whole-paper review, explicit no-fix outcomes, and bounded artifact-safe revision. Existing writing assistants, critique generators, and judge-centered loops lack durable issue identity across rounds, deterministic routing from critique to adjudication, and manuscript control that can reject invalid concerns or defer author-dependent ones. We present PaperJury, a closed-loop review-verdict-revise-verify system built on a deterministic-versus-semantic split: deterministic orchestration manages decomposition, a frozen claim spine, a durable ledger, routing, stopping, and exact-once patch application, while semantic agents are limited to bounded review, judgment, and repair. PaperJury combines bounded holistic review, contestability-based routing, a due-process trial, and risk-proportional guard chains for anchor-bounded edits, yielding terminal outcomes of invalid-drop, valid-fixable, and author-required. In a two-arm expert-review evaluation on held-out Vision, natural language processing, and machine learning papers against four baselines, we assess issue quality, verdict and routing quality, edit safety, convergence behavior, and cost, supporting the thesis that load-bearing safety and completion logic should reside in deterministic orchestration rather than model discretion. PaperJury is available at https://github.com/u7079256/paperjury.

</details>


### [349] [TMASC: Transmasculine Attitude and Speech Corpus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16351)
*Sidney Wong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The TMASC is a multimodal corpus of 196 transmasculine individuals, comprising questionnaire responses and audio recordings, aimed at supporting this community through various case studies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To support transmasculine individuals by providing a corpus that explores their vocal health and speech characteristics.

Method: Development of the TMASC, which includes collecting questionnaire responses and audio samples from transmasculine participants.

Result: Three case studies show the corpus's utility, demonstrating integration of data types, identification of group characteristics, and calibration of acoustic measurements.

Conclusion: The TMASC provides valuable insights and tools for understanding and supporting transmasculine vocal health.

Abstract: We introduce the Transmasculine Attitudes and Speech Corpus (TMASC), a multimodal corpus of 196 transmasculine individuals, including questionnaire responses and 66 audio recordings. The questionnaire includes items exploring the vocal health of transmasculine individuals. The audio recordings include cough and throat-clearing samples, a reading passage, and additional session-specific questions. This paper outlines the development of this corpus and the data collection procedures. To illustrate the utility of this corpus, we present three case studies demonstrating how this crowd-sourced multimodal corpus can be used to support transmasculine individuals. These include the integration of perceptual and acoustic data, the identification of group-level characteristics, and the calibration of acoustic measurements.

</details>


### [350] [Tyler: Typed Latent Reasoning for Language Models -- When to Think, What to Compute, and How Much to Allocate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16360)
*Hanyu Lin,Min Cai,Jiawei Wen,Haodi Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Tyler enhances latent reasoning in LLMs by optimizing when to invoke computations and how to allocate resources, improving performance significantly over CoT and other methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the limitations of existing latent reasoning methods which do not optimize when and how to employ latent computation in LLMs.

Method: Tyler proposes a policy that decides between generating text tokens and using a latent computation module tailored to specific reasoning functions during autoregressive decoding.

Result: Tyler demonstrates accuracy improvements of up to 14.49 points over CoT and 4.30 points over the strongest baseline across three backbone LLMs.

Conclusion: Tyler not only outperforms existing methods but also generalizes effectively across various reasoning tasks and exhibits minimal forgetting.

Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting improves reasoning in large language models (LLMs) by externalizing intermediate computation as discrete text tokens, but this textual interface also introduces redundancy and inference overhead. Latent reasoning offers a promising alternative by carrying part of the computation in continuous representations. However, existing methods typically predefine when latent computation is invoked and how it is allocated during decoding, leaving a key problem unresolved: when to invoke latent computation, what type of computation to perform, and how much budget to allocate. We propose \textbf{Ty}ped \textbf{L}at\textbf{e}nt \textbf{R}easoning (Tyler), a typed and budget-aware framework for latent reasoning during autoregressive decoding. Tyler learns a policy that, at each decoding step, chooses between emitting a text token and switching to a latent computation module specialized for a particular reasoning function. Once invoked, an operator maps the current reasoning state into latent tokens that support global planning, local state updates, or reusable procedural abstraction. Across extensive experiments on three backbone LLMs, Tyler improves accuracy by up to 14.49 points over CoT and by up to 4.30 points over the strongest competing baseline. It further generalizes across diverse reasoning domains and achieves the best final-stage performance with the lowest forgetting.

</details>


### [351] [Evaluating LLM Personalization via Semantic Constraint Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16368)
*Xuran Li,Guanqin Zhang,Imran Razzak,Hakim Hacid,Eleanna Kafeza,Hao Xue,Flora D. Salim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents NLICV, a new framework for evaluating LLM personalization based on semantic mapping and NLI models, enhancing interpretability and efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve evaluation methods for LLM personalization by addressing issues with existing surface-matching metrics and expensive judge protocols.

Method: NLICV maps sentence meanings to truth-condition sets and verifies constraints through an NLI model, categorizing LLM behaviors into four modes.

Result: NLICV shows strong alignment with human annotations and significantly reduces latency and cost of evaluations, achieving up to 2100 times speedup.

Conclusion: NLICV offers a more interpretable and efficient approach for evaluating LLMs, identifying key sentences in evaluation constraints.

Abstract: Current evaluation paradigms for Large Language Model (LLM) personalization rely heavily on brittle surface-matching metrics or computationally expensive LLM-as-a-judge protocols, both of which lack interpretability. To address these limitations, we introduce Natural Language Inference Constraint Verification (NLICV), a scalable, semantically invariant framework that maps sentence meanings to truth-condition sets to verify personalization constraints via a Natural Language Inference (NLI) model. Moving beyond binary scoring, NLICV categorizes LLM behaviors into four distinct modes: personalization, generalization, sycophancy, and failure. Extensive experiments demonstrate that NLICV aligns closely with human annotations while drastically reducing the latency and token costs associated with LLM judges (up to 2100 inference speedup). Finally, through an ablation-based procedure, NLICV pinpoints the exact sentences driving the constraint verification, yielding faithful, understandable evidence for its evaluations.

</details>


### [352] [Surpassing Scale by Efficiency: A Compact 135M Parameter Foundational LLM Natively Adapted for the Bangla Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16383)
*Rabindra Nath Nandi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces bangla-smollm-135m, a compact 135M parameter model for efficient language modeling in Bangla script, outperforming larger models in zero-shot tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the computational challenges of deploying large NLP models in low-resource, non-Latin scripts, particularly for edge environments.

Method: The model utilizes a deterministic intersect-and-append token merging strategy, enhancing token management without affecting pretrained parameters.

Result: In zero-shot benchmarks, bangla-smollm-135m performs on par with larger models (1B parameters) and surpasses models of twice its size.

Conclusion: bangla-smollm-135m is an efficient and effective model for Bangla language tasks, freely accessible for further research.

Abstract: While the NLP landscape is dominated by multi-billion parameter architectures, their deployment in low-resource, non-Latin scripts remains computationally prohibitive for edge configurations, mobile systems, and decentralized local hardware. This paper presents bangla-smollm-135m, a highly compact 135-million parameter decoder-only foundational model engineered explicitly for high-efficiency language modeling in the Bangla script. By leveraging a deterministic intersect-and-append token merging strategy between TituLLMs and SmolLM2-135M, the model overcomes subword script fragmentation without destabilizing early pretrained parameter states. In zero-shot multi-task benchmark evaluations (PIQA_bn, OpenBookQA_bn, CommonsenseQA_bn, and Bangla_MMLU), bangla-smollm-135m matches or outperforms models twice its size (Gemma-3-270m) and achieves parity with models in the 1B parameter tier. The model is available at rnnandi/bangla-smollm-135m

</details>


### [353] [A Mechanistic Understanding of Pronoun Fidelity in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16407)
*Katharina Trinley,Jesujoba O. Alabi,Dietrich Klakow,Vagrant Gautam*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper analyzes pronoun fidelity in language models through a mechanistic lens, identifying three causal mechanisms – group entity binding, recency bias, and stereotypical bias – that coexist and interact within the models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the shortcomings of large language models in maintaining faithful and coherent pronoun use, particularly in scenarios with multiple referents using different pronouns.

Method: The study employs a mechanistic approach to analyze the internal workings of language models, testing three identified mechanisms and their interaction using Boundless Distributed Alignment Search.

Result: The coexistence of group entity binding, recency bias, and stereotypical bias is confirmed across various language models, with no single mechanism fully explaining model behavior but a combination accounting for 91-99.5% of it.

Conclusion: Pronoun fidelity in language models is the result of competition between multiple active causal subspaces, with unique copying routes for different mechanisms.

Abstract: Faithful and robust pronoun use is important for fair and coherent generations, yet large language models largely fail when multiple referents use different pronouns. To study the interplay of reasoning, repetition, and bias in this task, prior work relies exclusively on behavioural approaches, which may not reflect a model's internal workings. Therefore, we provide a mechanistic, model-internal perspective on pronoun fidelity, testing whether three mechanisms -- group entity binding (G), recency bias (R), and stereotypical bias (S) -- are causally implemented across several SOTA language models. Using Boundless Distributed Alignment Search, we find all three coexist as causal subspaces distributed across network depth. No single mechanism fully explains model behaviour, but a combination of the three consistently accounts for 91-99.5%. An attention head analysis further reveals two competing copying routes; group binding and stereotype share a localized concept-level route that retrieves a bound occupation-pronoun unit, while recency uses a distributed token-level route that repeats surface forms. In sum, pronoun fidelity arises from competition between simultaneously active causal subspaces.

</details>


### [354] [PathRouter: Aligning Rewards with Retrieval Quality in Agentic Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16409)
*Bo Wang,Heyan Huang,Yaolin Li,Wei Tang,Yuan Zhang,Wenbo Li,Mingze Gao,Ge Shi,Chong Feng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: PathRouter enhances decision-making in graph-structured language models by addressing reward aliasing and search-update ambiguity, leading to improved accuracy in QA tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation behind this paper is to improve the decision-making capabilities of language-model agents navigating complex information networks by addressing inherent challenges in reinforcement learning.

Method: PathRouter is a training framework that categorizes trajectories based on answer correctness and evidence-path overlap, employing differentiated GRPO advantage scaling and token-level KL guidance from a frozen teacher model.

Result: PathRouter yields a significant F1 score improvement across various model sizes, demonstrating higher answer accuracy and better evidence-path overlapping compared to baseline methods.

Conclusion: The findings indicate that targeted training strategies can enhance agentic reasoning and evidence retrieval, achieving better performance in question-answering tasks.

Abstract: Agentic GraphRAG trains language-model agents to iteratively retrieve and reason over graph-structured evidence, enabling more accurate and context-aware decision-making by efficiently navigating complex information networks. However, outcome-only reinforcement learning suffers from \textit{\textbf{answer-path reward aliasing}}, where correct answers may come from shortcuts rather than useful evidence paths. It also exhibits \textit{\textbf{search-update ambiguity}}, as scalar trajectory-level feedback does not indicate which retrieval actions to adjust. To mitigate these shortcomings, we present PathRouter, a path-aware training framework for agentic GraphRAG. PathRouter jointly evaluates each trajectory along answer correctness and evidence-path overlap, yielding four trajectory categories with differentiated GRPO advantage scaling that suppresses shortcut reinforcement while preserving evidence-seeking behavior. For evidence-poor trajectories, a frozen gold-evidence teacher provides token-level KL guidance on reasoning and search-query tokens, excluding answer tokens to avoid direct response imitation. Experiments on six QA benchmarks across three model sizes show that PathRouter consistently improves answer F1 and evidence-path overlap, achieving average F1 gains of 3.1 on 3B and 4.9 on 7B models compared to a strong baseline.

</details>


### [355] [LectūraAgents: A Multi-Agent Framework for Adaptive Personalized AI-Assisted Learning and Embodied Teaching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16428)
*Jaward Sesay,Yue Yu,Siwei Dong,Yemin Shi,Guangyao Chen,Börje F. Karlsson*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LectūraAgents is a multi-agent framework for personalized AI-assisted learning that adapts instructional content to individual learners through a ProfessorAgent leading specialized subordinate agents, enhancing teaching through embodied methods and a unique alignment algorithm.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need for educational systems that can provide accurate, personalized, and dynamically adaptive instructions to diverse learners, moving beyond traditional content automation.

Method: LectūraAgents employs a hierarchical multi-agent architecture, where a ProfessorAgent coordinates a team of specialized agents to deliver tailored educational content through embodied teaching methods and the TASA algorithm.

Result: Experimental evaluations indicate significant improvements in the quality of lecture content, embodied teaching, assessment, and personalization compared to existing methods, validated through expert analysis.
